title: Strong winds spread a fire in California
summary:
A fast fire burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday, October 16. Strong winds pushed the fire, called the Norte Fire.

It started in the beach city of San Clemente. Then the wind carried it into the nearby city of San Juan Capistrano. About 16,000 people were told to leave their homes and go somewhere safe. Each city opened a shelter.

Firefighters sprayed water on homes. Two firefighters went to the hospital because of the heat. Officials do not yet know how the fire started.

The winds are called Santa Anas. They are dry, warm winds that blow toward the coast. The risk of fires was expected to stay high through Saturday night.

To help prevent fires, power companies turned off electricity for some people. More than 118,000 customers had no power. Nine schools in San Juan Capistrano were closed on Friday.
why_it_matters: Knowing why fires spread and why people leave home early helps families stay safe in an emergency.

keywords.explanation: A shelter is a safe place where people can stay during an emergency.

Santa Anas are dry, warm winds in Southern California that blow toward the coast.
Electricity is the power that runs lights and machines in homes and schools.
Customers are people or homes that pay a company for a service, like power.

background_read: Fires spread faster when plants are dry and strong winds blow sparks to new places.
When a fire comes close to homes, officials tell people to leave so they can stay safe while firefighters work.
Power companies sometimes turn off electricity in dry, windy weather so their equipment does not start a fire.
